subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The 'heuristic' function in Halliday's model is used to:
options: Explore and learn about the environment, often through questions
questions.explain: The heuristic function uses language to investigate the world, frequently via 'why' and 'what' questions.

questions.q: Which word class does 'quickly' belong to in 'She ran quickly'?
questions.explain: 'Quickly' modifies the verb 'ran', making it an adverb of manner.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'declarative' sentence used to give information?
questions.explain: Declaratives make statements with typical subject-verb word order, here conveying factual information.

questions.q: In phonological development, voiced sounds and front consonants like /p/, /b/, /m/ tend to be acquired:
questions.explain: Bilabial and other front consonants such as /p/, /b/, /m/ are typically among the earliest sounds children produce.

questions.q: Anaphoric reference occurs when a pronoun:
options: Points forward to something mentioned later
Points back to something already mentioned
questions.explain: Anaphora refers back to a previously stated noun phrase, e.g. 'Sam arrived; he was late' where 'he' refers back to 'Sam'.

questions.q: A 'semantic field' is best described as:
options: The set of sounds in a language
A space left blank on a page
A clause acting as the subject
A group of words linked by a shared area of meaning
questions.explain: A semantic field (or lexical field) is a set of words related by topic, such as 'pitch', 'goal' and 'striker' in football.

questions.q: The two-word stage is significant because it marks the first appearance of:
questions.explain: At the two-word stage children begin combining words in consistent order, showing early grammatical/syntactic awareness.

questions.q: Berko's 'wug test' demonstrated that young children can:
options: Apply grammatical rules such as plural -s to invented words
questions.explain: In Berko's study children added the plural -s to the nonsense word 'wug', showing they had internalised the rule, not merely memorised forms.

questions.q: In linguistic analysis, the term 'graphology' refers to the study of which aspect of a text?
options: The visual and presentational features such as layout, font and colour
The personality of the writer revealed by handwriting
The sounds and their physical articulation
questions.explain: In language study graphology denotes the visual aspects of a text (typography, layout, images), not the popular pseudoscience of handwriting analysis.

questions.q: The telegraphic stage of development is characterised by utterances that:
options: Are grammatically complete with all inflections
Use three or more words while omitting function words like determiners and auxiliaries
questions.explain: Telegraphic speech (around 24-36 months) strings content words together, e.g. 'Daddy throw ball', leaving out grammatical function words.

questions.q: A 'subordinating conjunction' such as 'although' or 'because' functions to:
options: Join two grammatically equal main clauses
Introduce a subordinate clause that depends on a main clause
questions.explain: Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses; coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) join equal elements.

questions.q: The words 'here', 'now' and 'you' are examples of deixis because their meaning:
options: Is purely grammatical with no reference
Can only occur in written mode
Depends on the context of utterance such as place, time or speaker
questions.explain: Deictic terms point to features of the utterance context (spatial, temporal or personal) and cannot be interpreted without it.

questions.q: In the noun phrase 'the very old wooden chair', the word 'chair' functions as the:
questions.explain: The head is the central, obligatory word of the phrase; 'the very old wooden' are modifiers premodifying the head 'chair'.

questions.q: Which theorist proposed an innate 'Language Acquisition Device' (LAD)?
questions.explain: Chomsky's nativist theory argues children possess an innate LAD enabling rapid grammar acquisition from limited input.

questions.q: Which discourse feature is a 'discourse marker'?
questions.explain: Discourse markers such as 'well', 'right' and 'anyway' organise and signal shifts in spoken or written discourse.

questions.q: In Brown and Levinson's politeness theory, 'negative face' refers to a person's desire to:
options: Be free from imposition and have their autonomy respected
Be liked and approved of by others
questions.explain: Negative face is the want to be unimpeded and autonomous; positive face is the want to be approved of and included.

questions.q: Bruner's concept of the 'Language Acquisition Support System' (LASS) refers to:
options: The supportive interaction and scaffolding provided by caregivers
An innate device inside the child's brain
questions.explain: Bruner's LASS stresses the role of adult interaction, routines and scaffolding in supporting a child's language development.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the nativist position on a 'critical period' for language?
options: Language can be acquired equally easily at any age
Only writing has a critical period
Language is purely learned through reward
There is a biologically optimal window in early childhood for acquiring language
questions.explain: The critical period hypothesis (associated with Lenneberg) holds that there is an early window during which language is most readily acquired.

questions.q: Which is the most accurate description of 'phonology' as opposed to 'phonetics'?
options: Phonology studies how sounds function and pattern in a language; phonetics studies the physical properties of sounds
Phonology studies the physical production of speech sounds; phonetics studies sound systems
questions.explain: Phonetics deals with the physical articulation/acoustics of speech sounds, while phonology studies how sounds function within a particular language system.

questions.q: Skinner's behaviourist account of language acquisition emphasises:
questions.explain: Skinner argued children learn language through imitation and operant conditioning, with correct utterances reinforced by carers.

questions.q: A 'virtuous error' is so termed because it:
options: Reveals the child applying a logical rule, even if the result is non-standard
Shows the child is morally good
questions.explain: Virtuous errors like 'sheeps' or 'runned' reflect intelligent rule application, evidencing active learning rather than careless mistakes.

questions.q: The phonological simplification whereby 'spoon' becomes 'poon' is called:
questions.explain: Cluster reduction simplifies consonant clusters by deleting one consonant, e.g. /sp/ reduced to /p/ in 'poon'.

questions.q: In analysing mode, electronic communication such as instant messaging is often described as:
options: Purely written with no spoken features
Occupying a position on a continuum, blending spoken and written features
questions.explain: Electronically mediated communication blends speech-like immediacy with written form, sitting between the spoken and written ends of a mode continuum.

questions.q: Halliday's 'regulatory' function of child language is used to:
options: Influence or control the behaviour of others
questions.explain: The regulatory function gives directions to control others, e.g. 'do that again', whereas the interactional maintains relationships.

questions.q: In the development of writing, Kroll's stages place which stage first?
questions.explain: Kroll's model begins with the preparatory stage (developing motor skills and the basic principles of the writing system).

questions.q: In Lakoff's and later politeness research, a 'hedge' such as 'sort of' or 'maybe' functions to:
options: Soften or mitigate the force of an utterance
Mark the end of a turn
Increase the force of a statement
questions.explain: Hedges reduce the directness or assertiveness of an utterance, often to protect face or signal tentativeness.

questions.q: The order in which children acquire grammatical morphemes (e.g. -ing before regular plural -s before past -ed) was studied by:
questions.explain: Roger Brown documented a relatively consistent order of acquisition of grammatical morphemes in young children.

questions.q: In lexical analysis, 'denotation' refers to:
options: The literal, primary dictionary meaning of a word
questions.explain: Denotation is the explicit, definitional meaning of a word, contrasted with its connotative associations.

questions.q: A child who uses the word 'cup' only for their own special cup and no other cups is showing:
questions.explain: Under-extension restricts a word's meaning to fewer referents than the adult use allows.

questions.q: In Grice's Cooperative Principle, the maxim of 'quantity' requires a speaker to:
options: Make a contribution as informative as required, but no more
Be brief, orderly and avoid obscurity
questions.explain: The maxim of quantity concerns giving the right amount of information; quality concerns truth, relation relevance, and manner clarity.
